subtitle: Stateful agent graphs on a real domain: nodes, edges, checkpointing, and human-in-the-loop for order flows, returns, and support — LangGraph applied, not toyed
audience: Developers who finished Prompt Engineering 101 (prompt packs feed graph nodes directly) and want agents with memory, branches, and approval gates instead of single-shot prompts. All graph machinery is taught twice: once as runnable pure-JS miniatures in the JS Playground, once as real @langchain/langgraph code for your Node project.
outcomes: Model agent work as graphs (nodes, edges, shared state) instead of chains or monolith prompts
Design state schemas with reducers so parallel and repeated updates merge predictably
Write node functions (lookup, decide, draft) with typed inputs and contract-shaped outputs
Route with conditional edges and validate every branch with routing tests
Persist threads with checkpointers: resume, replay, and time-travel debugging
Gate risky actions behind human-in-the-loop interrupts with approve/edit/skip flows
Give nodes tools and structured output with schema-validated arguments
Compose subgraphs and choose supervisor vs sequential patterns deliberately
Evaluate graphs with trace replay and conversation gold sets
Ship a returns-resolution graph: triage → policy → draft → approval → log, measured

assessment.q: Chains vs graphs for 'triage → policy → draft → approval' — why graphs?
options: Branches, loops, shared state, and gates need nodes + conditional edges; chains express only fixed sequences
assessment.explain: Control flow decides: linear fixed work fits chains; branching/looping/gated work needs graph topology (Ch.1).

assessment.q: Two nodes append messages to state.messages concurrently. Correct design?
options: A reducer (concat/merge) on the channel so updates compose predictably regardless of order
assessment.explain: Shared mutable state needs merge semantics: reducers make concurrent/sequential updates order-safe (Ch.2).

assessment.q: Node returns {approved: 'yes'} but the contract wants boolean. Where is this caught?
options: Schema validation at the node boundary (Zod): quarantine with evidence, never silent coercion downstream
assessment.explain: Node outputs are untrusted input to the graph: validate at boundaries with the OpenDataLoader discipline applied to agent state (Ch.3).

assessment.q: Router sends 5% of refunds to the wrong branch. First check?
options: Routing tests: enumerated inputs × expected branch, run on every router edit — branch coverage for graphs
assessment.explain: Routers are pure functions of state: test them like functions with branch coverage, not vibes (Ch.4).

assessment.q: Support run must pause for manager approval over $100, then resume exactly. Mechanism?
options: interrupt() before the action + checkpointer persistence: resume re-enters post-approval with full state
assessment.explain: HITL = interrupt + durable state. Checkpointing makes resume exact; approval edits state before continuation (Ch.5–6).

assessment.q: Checkpoint writes on every step feel expensive. Response?
options: Checkpoint on thread-scoped, bounded state with per-step writes measured; cost is durability for resume/replay/audit — scope state minimally instead
assessment.explain: Durability is the product (resume, replay, audit). Control cost by scoping state and measuring, not by dropping persistence (Ch.5).

assessment.q: Tool call ships {amount: 'ten'} for a numeric schema. Handling?
options: Schema-validate tool args at the boundary; quarantine failures with evidence for repair-or-escalate
assessment.explain: Tool args are contracts: validate, quarantine with evidence, repair or escalate explicitly. Silent coercion corrupts money flows (Ch.7).

assessment.q: Returns flow reused by three parent graphs. Shape?
options: Subgraph: named, versioned, independently tested unit composed into parents
assessment.explain: Subgraphs are functions for graphs: reuse without duplication, tested once, versioned (Ch.8).

assessment.q: Supervisor vs sequential multi-agent for returns + fraud + VIP handling?
options: Supervisor when routing needs judgment per step; sequential when the pipeline is fixed — match topology to control-flow needs
assessment.explain: Topology follows control flow: dynamic delegation → supervisor; fixed pipeline → sequential. (Ch.8; CrewAI course goes deeper on teams.)

assessment.q: Graph passes unit tests but fails on real tickets. Missing eval layer?
options: Conversation gold sets + trace replay on real tickets: end-to-end behavior with per-node attribution, not just node correctness
assessment.explain: Node tests don't cover composition. Trace replay attributes failures to nodes/routers/state across realistic conversations (Ch.9).

assessment.q: v2 graph beats v1 overall but regresses VIP handling. Process?
options: Per-segment diffs on the same conversation set; fix VIP path before shipping — aggregates hide localized regressions
assessment.explain: Segment-level diffs (Prompt 101 Ch.7 discipline applied to graphs): same set, item attribution, no shipping with known regressions (Ch.9).

assessment.q: Human edits state at an interrupt, then resumes. What must hold?
options: Edits conform to the state schema (validated) and resume continues from the interrupt point with edited state — approval-with-changes as first-class flow
assessment.explain: Edit-and-resume is the HITL power move: validated edits, exact continuation. Design interrupts expecting edits, not just approvals (Ch.6).

project.title: The Returns-Resolution Graph
project.summary: Ship a working returns-resolution agent graph for a shoe store: ticket triage with routing tests, policy-grounded decisions, drafted replies with contracts, human approval over $100, full checkpointing, and an evaluation report with per-segment diffs. The capstone that turns prompt packs into stateful agents.
requirements: State schema: ticket, facts, decision, draft, approval, log — with reducers where updates merge
Nodes: triage (router-tested), policy lookup, decide (contract-shaped), draft (≤60 words), approval gate (interrupt over $100), logger
Conditional edges: segment routing with enumerated routing tests (all branches covered)
Checkpointing: thread-scoped persistence; demonstrate resume + one replayed trace
HITL: interrupt flow with approve/edit/skip paths demonstrated on a $100+ case
Evaluation: 12-conversation gold set (happy/edge/attack), baseline scores overall + per-segment, one iterated fix with delta
technical: Graph machinery in runnable JS (playground-compatible runner) plus real @langchain/langgraph code for Node
Node outputs schema-validated (Zod-style) with quarantine on violations
Threads isolated by ID; checkpoints bounded in size (state scoped minimally)
All numbers reproducible: gold set + router tests committed
project.architecture: Four sections: (1) Graph map — nodes/edges/state diagram with routing table; (2) Runs — three traced conversations (happy, edge, interrupt) with per-node attribution; (3) Evaluation — gold scores, per-segment diffs, iterated fix with delta; (4) Operations — checkpoint policy, approval audit log design, guardrails carried from Prompt 101.
steps: Design state + routing table on paper; write routing tests first
Build nodes with contracts (reuse Prompt 101 pack pieces as node prompts)
Wire edges, add interrupt + checkpointer; demonstrate approve/edit/skip
Build the 12-conversation gold set; baseline; iterate one variable; re-score
Write the operations section; self-review against failure modes (Prompt 101 Ch.9)
evaluation: All branches routing-tested; router coverage 100% on enumerated inputs
Interrupt demonstrated with state intact across resume; edit path shown
Gold baseline + one iteration with per-segment diffs on the same set
No silent defaults anywhere; quarantine paths demonstrated or documented
State scoped and bounded; checkpoint policy stated
stretch: Add a fraud-check subgraph composed into the returns graph with its own tests
Benchmark checkpointed vs uncheckpointed runs and report the overhead honestly
Convert one node to tool-calling (order lookup tool) with schema-validated args

interviewQs.q: When do agents need graphs instead of chains?
interviewQs.a: When control flow branches (triage routing), loops (verify→redraft), shares evolving state across steps, or gates on humans/tools. Chains express fixed sequences; graphs express decisions, repetition, and collaboration. The test: if you can delete the router and nothing breaks, a chain sufficed — otherwise the topology earns its keep.

interviewQs.q: State design: what goes in, what stays out?
interviewQs.a: In: everything downstream steps need (facts, decisions, drafts, approvals, logs) with merge reducers for shared channels. Out: raw bulk (full manuals — pass references/IDs), secrets beyond need, unbounded histories (summarize into rolling state). Bounded, typed, minimal state keeps checkpoints cheap and resumes exact.

interviewQs.q: How do you test a conditional-edge router?
interviewQs.a: As a pure function: enumerated inputs × expected branch, covering every edge including fallbacks and adversarial inputs (injection attempts routing to quarantine). Run on every router edit; branch coverage is the metric. Routers are the highest-leverage test target in a graph — small code, total control-flow authority.

interviewQs.q: Interrupt design for a $100+ refund approval?
interviewQs.a: interrupt() before the side-effecting node with full checkpointed state; surface ticket+decision+draft to the approver; support approve/edit/skip with validated edits; resume continues exactly; log every path including skips. Design expecting edits (approval-with-changes), not just binary approvals — and never place interrupts after irreversible actions.

Per-step writes buy resume-after-failure, exact replay for debugging, time-travel during development, and audit trails for money-adjacent actions. Control cost by scoping state minimally and measuring; never by dropping persistence on stateful flows. Stateless retries re-run blind — checkpoints make failures resumable and debuggable.

interviewQs.q: Supervisor vs sequential agents — decide for order support.
interviewQs.a: Sequential for fixed pipelines (triage→decide→draft→log always in order): simpler, cheaper, debuggable. Supervisor when steps need dynamic choice (fraud check sometimes, VIP handling sometimes, escalation on signals). Match topology to control-flow variability; decompose into subgraphs (returns, fraud) either way for reuse and independent testing.
